questions.q: What are this course's three flagship projects, in order?
options: A full DeFi protocol, an NFT marketplace, and a DAO governance system
A blog platform, a chat app, and a game
Three separate DeFi protocols with no variation
A DAO, then a DeFi protocol, then career prep only
questions.explain: The course builds a DeFi protocol (Project 1), an NFT marketplace (Project 2), and a DAO governance system (Project 3), followed by a career-preparation chapter.

questions.q: A student targeting a full-stack Web3 developer role is deciding which project to polish deepest. Per this lesson's framework, which should they pick?
options: The NFT marketplace, since it leans on escrow patterns, indexing, and marketplace UX
The DAO, since all roles need governance expertise
Whichever project is shortest to build
It doesn't matter which project a developer polishes
questions.explain: The lesson's framework matches project emphasis to target role, and the NFT marketplace's indexing and frontend/UX work most closely mirrors full-stack Web3 developer responsibilities.

questions.q: How does this contract track each liquidity provider's claim on the pool?
options: With a plain mapping(address => uint256), not a minted ERC-20 LP token
By minting a separate transferable ERC-20 LP token, exactly like a production AMM
It doesn't track individual claims at all
By storing claims in an off-chain database
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this teaching version uses a plain mapping for shares instead of minting a real transferable LP token, trading that feature away for a contract that's easier to read in full.

questions.q: Before deploying to Sepolia, what does this lesson say about the wallet you should use?
options: A dedicated testnet-only wallet, funded from a public faucet — never a wallet that has ever held real funds
Your personal mainnet wallet, since testnets are completely isolated anyway
Any wallet works equally well; the choice doesn't matter
A wallet borrowed from a classmate
questions.explain: The pre-deploy checklist is explicit: use a dedicated testnet-only wallet funded from a faucet, and never reuse a wallet that has ever held real funds.

questions.q: What does useWriteContract do, per this lesson?
options: Sends a state-changing transaction through the connected wallet and tracks its pending/success/error status
Only reads data without ever requiring a wallet signature
Deletes a deployed contract from the blockchain
Compiles Solidity source code in the browser
questions.explain: useWriteContract is the wagmi hook used to send state-changing calls like swapAforB through the user's connected wallet, with the wallet prompting a signature and the hook exposing transaction status.

questions.q: Which network does this project's contract get deployed to, per this lesson?
options: Ethereum mainnet, using a wallet that holds real funds
The Sepolia testnet, never a wallet holding real funds
A private local-only network with no public access ever
No deployment happens in this project
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that deployment targets the Sepolia testnet and that the project should never use a wallet that holds real funds.

questions.q: In this capstone's scope, how does a listed NFT stay with its owner?
options: It doesn't -- it's always transferred into the marketplace contract immediately
The owner mails a signed paper deed to the marketplace
The seller only grants the marketplace an approval; the NFT itself stays in the seller's wallet until it sells
The NFT is burned and re-minted after sale
questions.explain: This project uses an approval-based pattern: the seller approves the marketplace contract to transfer the NFT later, but keeps holding it until a sale actually completes.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is generally more valuable in a portfolio than a long list of projects?
options: A small number of complete, well-documented projects with answers ready for their specific tradeoffs
The total number of GitHub repositories, regardless of completeness
Having every project written in a different blockchain framework
Avoiding any discussion of tradeoffs to appear more confident
questions.explain: This closes the loop with the point made back in Chapter 1: depth over breadth -- a few fully-finished, well-documented projects demonstrate real engineering ability better than many shallow ones.

questions.q: What does parseEther do in the listing flow?
options: Fetches the current ETH/USD exchange rate
Converts a human-readable price string like "0.5" into the wei-denominated uint256 the contract's listItem expects
Signs the transaction on behalf of the user
Converts wei back into a human-readable string
questions.explain: parseEther converts a decimal ETH amount into the integer wei value Solidity's uint256 price parameter expects; formatEther does the reverse conversion when displaying a price.

questions.q: Why doesn't SimpleNFTMarketplace have a function that returns every active listing?
options: Storing and iterating an open-ended on-chain list gets expensive fast -- this is the general indexing problem, applied to this contract
Solidity doesn't allow mappings to be queried at all
It was simply forgotten in Lesson 9
Active listings are stored off-chain from the moment they're created
questions.explain: Marketplace contracts deliberately avoid storing and iterating unbounded lists on-chain because of gas cost; the contract instead emits events, and an indexer builds the queryable view.

questions.q: Why doesn't a flash-loan-style attack work against this project's voting mechanism?
options: Voting power is checkpointed at a snapshot block, so tokens borrowed right before a vote had no recorded weight at that snapshot
Flash loans are technically impossible on any EVM-compatible network
The Governor contract rejects all transactions from smart contract wallets
Voting power is based on the number of days since a wallet was created
questions.explain: The lesson explains checkpointed (not live) balances are specifically what defeats this kind of attack.

questions.q: A holder mints and receives governance tokens but never calls delegate(). What is their voting power on a proposal?
options: Zero, because ERC20Votes tracks voting power per delegate, not automatically per holder
Equal to their full token balance automatically
Double their token balance
Negative, as a penalty for not delegating
questions.explain: The lesson calls out forgetting to delegate as the most common reason a new governance token appears to report zero voting power in testing.

questions.q: What does renouncing the deployer's TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE after setup actually accomplish?
options: It removes the deployer's ability to grant themselves proposer or executor rights and bypass governance entirely
It permanently locks the treasury so no proposal can ever execute
It transfers all treasury funds to the deployer
It has no real effect and is purely symbolic
questions.explain: The lesson calls this the step that actually makes the system decentralized -- without it, a standing admin could bypass the vote at any time.

questions.q: What is the final step in the deployment sequence, and why does it matter?
options: Renouncing the deployer's TIMELOCK_ADMIN_ROLE, which finishes the handoff to on-chain governance
Minting additional governance tokens to the deployer
Deleting the Governor contract's source code
Setting the voting period to zero
questions.explain: The lesson calls renouncing the admin role the step that finishes the handoff -- without it the deployer retains a standing backdoor.

questions.q: In the lesson's suggested one-page structure, what comes right after the header and optional summary?
options: The three capstone projects, each with proof-backed bullets and a verification link
A full list of every programming language ever studied
References from previous employers
A certificate gallery with no further detail
questions.explain: The structure places the three capstone projects early, since they carry the strongest, most specific proof of ability.

questions.q: Which section does the lesson say most directly influences a hiring decision, and why?
options: Key design decisions, because a reviewer can run the tests themselves but can't read your reasoning anywhere else
The software license section, because legal compliance is the top hiring factor
The getting-started install steps, since no other part of a README matters as much
The contributors list, since team size is the main signal reviewers look for
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out the design-decisions section as the one that most influences hiring, since reasoning isn't otherwise visible.

questions.q: Why is using tx.origin for authorization considered a known vulnerability?
options: A malicious intermediate contract can trick a legitimate user into a call where tx.origin still reflects that user
tx.origin always returns the zero address, breaking all authorization checks
tx.origin is not a real field available in the EVM
tx.origin changes on every single function call within one transaction
questions.explain: The lesson explains the risk precisely: tx.origin reflects the original EOA regardless of how many contracts the call passed through, which an attacker can exploit.

questions.q: In Exercise 2's unstake function, what effect does wrapping the subtraction in an unchecked block have?
options: It disables Solidity's default underflow protection, letting the value wrap instead of reverting
It automatically doubles the gas cost of the function
It makes the function impossible to call successfully
It has no effect, since unchecked blocks are purely cosmetic
questions.explain: The lesson explains unchecked disables the default revert-on-underflow behavior, letting an excessive amount wrap to a huge number instead.

questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid quoting a specific blockchain salary figure?
options: Salary figures go stale fast and vary by market, and this catalog has no reliable way to verify one as current -- so it teaches the research process instead
Blockchain roles are never compensated with a salary of any kind
Salary negotiation is not relevant to blockchain engineering roles
Specific numbers are illegal to discuss in a career-prep course
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly explains that it teaches a research process rather than quoting a number that could already be wrong or inapplicable to a reader's market.
